The Almighty
thee ahl-MY-tee
noun
Hebrew Shaddai (H7706) often combined with El (God) to form El Shaddai; Greek Pantokratōr (G3841) — "All-Ruling"; the Name of God emphasizing His omnipotent sovereignty, frequent in Job and in Revelation.

📖 Biblical Definition

The Almighty is one of God's great Names — the Name of His OMNIPOTENT SOVEREIGNTY over all that exists. The Hebrew El Shaddai appears 48 times in the Old Testament, almost exclusively in patriarchal narrative (Gen 17:1; 28:3; 35:11; 48:3) and in Job (31 times — the book where God's sovereignty is most relentlessly defended). The Greek Pantokratōr ("All-Ruling") translates Shaddai in the LXX and dominates the Book of Revelation, appearing 9 times in Revelation alone (1:8; 4:8; 11:17; 15:3; 16:7, 14; 19:6, 15; 21:22). "I am Alpha and Omega, the beginning and the ending, saith the Lord, which is, and which was, and which is to come, the Almighty" (Rev 1:8) — the climactic divine self-identification of the entire canon, applied to Christ. The four living creatures around the throne sing "Holy, holy, holy, Lord God Almighty" (Rev 4:8) — eternal worship of the All-Ruling One. The Name carries a specific theological weight: it is the Name God reveals when He calls Abraham to walk before Him and be perfect (Gen 17:1), when He blesses Jacob (Gen 35:11), and when His people need assurance that NO force can thwart His covenant. The Almighty cannot be overruled, outflanked, surprised, or defeated. Every promise He makes is backed by omnipotence. Every threat He utters is enforceable. The Christian's confidence rests not on his own strength but on the Name of the One whose strength is by definition exhaustless.

📜 Webster 1828 Definition

God's Name emphasizing His omnipotent sovereignty; Hebrew El Shaddai, Greek Pantokratōr; the All-Ruling One who cannot be overruled.

THE ALMIGHTY, noun. A Name of God emphasizing His omnipotent sovereignty. Hebrew El Shaddai ("God Almighty"), Greek Pantokratōr ("All-Ruling").

Frequent in patriarchal narrative (Gen 17:1; 28:3; 35:11; 48:3) and in Job (31 times); dominates Revelation (9 times — Rev 1:8; 4:8; 11:17; 15:3; 16:7, 14; 19:6, 15; 21:22).

📖 Key Scripture

Revelation 1:8 — "I am Alpha and Omega, the beginning and the ending, saith the Lord, which is, and which was, and which is to come, the Almighty."

Genesis 17:1 — "And when Abram was ninety years old and nine, the LORD appeared to Abram, and said unto him, I am the Almighty God; walk before me, and be thou perfect."

Revelation 4:8 — "And the four beasts had each of them six wings about him; and they were full of eyes within: and they rest not day and night, saying, Holy, holy, holy, Lord God Almighty, which was, and is, and is to come."

Job 11:7 — "Canst thou by searching find out God? canst thou find out the Almighty unto perfection?"

⚠️ Modern Corruption

The Almighty is corrupted when modernist theology shrinks God's sovereignty (open theism, process theology, neo-classical limited-God systems), or when prosperity theology turns omnipotence into a wealth-distribution machine rather than the ground of covenant assurance.

expand to see more

Sovereignty-shrinking theologies. Open theism, process theology, and various "limited God" systems all soften the Almighty's omnipotence — God doesn't know the future, God grows along with creation, God's power is bounded by libertarian human will, etc. Each system makes God less than the canonical Almighty. The biblical Pantokrator is ALL-RULING — He doesn't share rule, doesn't grow, doesn't get surprised. Christian assurance rests on this; if God can be thwarted, no promise of His is secure. Modern attempts to make God more "relatable" by shrinking Him actually destroy the gospel's confidence.

Prosperity-distortion. The prosperity gospel often invokes the Almighty as a power-source for personal wealth — "the Almighty God will bless you with abundance." But canonical use of the Name is in covenant contexts ("walk before me and be thou perfect," Gen 17:1) and worship contexts (Rev 4:8). The Almighty is invoked as the ground of God's covenant fidelity and as the object of unceasing worship — not as a wealth-machine. Strip the Name of its covenantal and doxological context and you have made an idol of power-as-personal-resource.
